Both have the woman tell her friend, before he goes, that she cannot live through his going (நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு; தம் இன்றி யாம் உயிர் வாழும் மதுகை இலேம் ... தம்மொடு போயின்று, சொல், என் உயிர்). The sleep-talk detail is accurate. But she still asks the friend to tell him (சொல்), so 'a woman who has already lost the chance to plead' misdescribes the poem, and the motive of sparing his name rests on the unclear பழி நிற்ப.
links.text_issue: Line 11 of Kalittokai 24 is supplied from sangamtamil.com.

links.reason: Both measure gossip by a Pandiyan-Kongar war cry with the same words (ஆர்ப்பினும் பெரிதே): the victory cheer at Kudal (கொங்கர் ஓட்டி ... கூடல் ஆடிய இன்இசை ஆர்ப்பு) and the Kongar's shout when Athikan fell at Vaakai. This is a real puram connection and the teaches is accurate, but neither poem limits the other; it is a shared figure.

Kuruntokai 80 uses Ezhini's war-front herds as the measure of guarding (பல்வேல் எழினி முனையான் பெருநிரை போலக் ... காக்க), and Purananuru 230 makes Ezhini the protector under whom herds rested unguarded (கன்று அமர் ஆயம் கானத்து அல்கவும் ... காப்பில வைகவும்). Nothing in the Tamil shows the two Ezhinis are the same man, and 230's herds need no guard while 80's must be guarded, a difference the note does not take up.

Tirumanthiram 7 has the god become what he is called (தன்னைஅப் பாயெனில் அப்பனு மாயுளன்) and fixes him as eldest (மூவர்க்கும் மூத்தவன்); Paripadal 2 makes Thirumal younger or elder as the worshipper says (இளையன் என்போர்க்கு இளையை ... முதியை என்போர்க்கு முதுமை தோன்றலும்). The Paripadal applies the same rule to seniority, which the Tirumanthiram fixes.

Both use a verb of giving for the girl causing his pain (கெடலரும் துயரம் நல்கி; தந்தாள் மடலொடு மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்), which is accurate. But Ainkurunuru 195 has no addressee and no plea to the friend, and nothing makes it an earlier stage of the couplet's complaint, so the 'stages' are invented on top of a shared topic.

poems.note: Line 3 (செயலையம் பகைத்தழி வாடும்) is obscure; the withering ashoka is a look, not an act.
The cloud and the eyes are joined openly (காரோடு அலமரும் ... நீரோடு அலமரும் கண்).

iraicchi.act: having lost its old strength of flight, the grieving heron sits on a bough that dips into the waves
iraicchi.sense: like the heron she has lost her former beauty and can only stay waiting at the shore of the man who took it

poems.note: The vengai is the poem's direct subject (did he forget it), so it cannot be struck.

iraicchi.act: the anril, the bird that calls for its mate at night, alone keeps her company and talks with her through the long watches
iraicchi.sense: her night is one of separation like the paired bird's, and no person shares her grief

iraicchi.act: the red-legged cock dove under the eaves calls its beloved mate in a helpless voice
iraicchi.sense: even the dove cries for its mate, so the man who leaves will leave her crying the same way, and he should not go

carrier: மடப் பிணை தழீஇய மா எருத்து இரலை
iraicchi.act: the stag embraces its young doe and rests with her in the striped shade of the velam
iraicchi.sense: the man stays with her as the stag stays with its doe, which is why he has given up the journey

poems.note: Two pairs: the langur breaking open the jackfruit is the lover's union, and its scent filling the little village is the gossip of line 3.
The startled horse is the chariot's own and part of the literal scene; only one correspondence (false alarm, gossip) can be drawn.

iraicchi.act: the tusker tears the bark of the yaa tree to ease the hunger of its herd
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees a beast provide for its own on his road will think of the one he left and come back

poems.note: The wife maps each quail fight to his affairs aloud, so the comparison is open.

iraicchi.act: the frightened she-elephant cries without sleep for her mate caught by the python
iraicchi.sense: the man crossing that forest will hear a mate grieving for its partner, so he will think of her grief and keep faith, as she says he will

poems.note: The turtle carrying its sleeping young could map to the wife and son, but no such situation is stated in the poem and there is no thurai.
